idiom_name: typed plugin contract plus dynamic import() with runtime schema validation
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds only the compile-time half of the pattern: the contract is published as an exported interface (often wrapped in a definePlugin helper that infers the shape), and the plugin's package.json - types, exports, and a peer dependency on the contract package - is its descriptor, but types are erased at run time, so the host must validate the loaded object with a schema or guard before trusting it. What replaces the classic structure is the same registry-plus-context object as in JavaScript, with the HostContext type controlling which host services a plugin can even see, and a semver range the plugin declares for the host version. When the extension set is known at build time, importing the implementations statically at the composition root gives full type checking and no load step - that is the trade for giving up add-without-recompiling.
pitfalls: A cast such as `as Plugin` compiles but proves nothing at run time; without schema validation a plugin with the wrong shape fails at the first call site instead of at load.

If host and plugin each depend on their own copy of the contract package, structurally identical types become nominally incompatible at compile time (and duplicate runtime state at run time) - the contract package belongs in peerDependencies.

Dynamic import specifiers are resolved at run time, so bundlers either fail or try to inline them; plugin paths must be runtime values and the plugin must be shipped as a separate module to the bundle.
